hypothesis: KDP crystals grown at 35°C with a slow cooling rate of 0.5°C/hour will yield larger, higher-purity crystals compared to faster cooling rates
context: KDP (potassium dihydrogen phosphate) crystallizes optimally during slow, controlled cooling from a supersaturated solution. This run establishes a baseline for slow-cooling methodology. The critical window is hours 2-6 when nucleation occurs — thermal shock during this phase causes crystal cracking and polycrystalline growth. pH must stay near neutral because KDP hydrolyzes above 7.5, which is irreversible. Rising impurity typically indicates crystal dissolution back into solution and correlates with temperature excursions.

stages.name: equilibration
stages.description: Hold at 35°C. Allow solution to reach thermal and chemical steady state. Impurity readings may be slightly elevated (up to 25 ppm) during this phase — this is normal and not a reason to intervene.

stages.name: nucleation
stages.description: Critical phase. Slow cooling begins at 0.5°C/hour. Crystals nucleate and begin growing. Do NOT make large temperature adjustments — treat warning_above as critical during this stage. Any thermal shock risks cracking the forming crystal lattice.

stages.name: growth
stages.description: Crystals growing at lower temperature. Monitor impurity closely — a rise here indicates dissolution. Capture microscopy images every 30 minutes to track crystal morphology.

temperature_c.concern: High temp dissolves crystals back into solution and raises impurity. Low temp causes rapid uncontrolled nucleation and polycrystalline growth. During nucleation stage (hours 2-6), treat warning_above as critical — do not wait for the critical threshold.

impurity_ppm.concern: Rising impurity means crystals are dissolving. Almost always correlates with a temperature excursion. If impurity rises alongside temperature, correct the temperature first — impurity will follow. An isolated impurity spike without a temperature cause may indicate external contamination.

ph.concern: pH above 7.5 causes KDP hydrolysis — this is irreversible and terminates the run. pH below 6.6 promotes phosphate precipitation. A slow drift of 0.1 over 2 hours is normal probe behavior. A sudden jump of more than 0.3 in a single reading suggests contamination or probe malfunction.

temperature_high.note: Never reduce more than 1°C per cycle. Thermal shock from overcorrection is worse than the excursion itself. Wait one full cycle (60s) to observe effect before adjusting again.

temperature_low.note: Warm slowly. Rapid reheating dissolves nucleated crystals. Only intervene if below warning_below for two consecutive readings.

ph_high.note: Start with 5ml, wait 60s, re-read before adding more. If pH is at or above critical_above, alert researcher immediately regardless of buffer action.

ph_low.note: Start conservative. If pH drops suddenly (>0.3 in one reading), alert researcher — this may indicate a contamination event rather than gradual drift.

impurity_spike.note: Lower temp slightly to encourage re-crystallization. Do not treat impurity in isolation — always check temperature first. If temperature is nominal, alert researcher rather than acting unilaterally.

known_risks: Impurity readings in hours 2-4 are typically elevated during nucleation onset — values up to 25 ppm are expected and not a reason to intervene.
Temperature control lags 2-3 minutes after a setpoint change — wait a full cycle before re-adjusting or you will overcorrect.
pH probe readings drift by ~0.05 per hour after 4+ hours of operation — slow monotonic drift is normal; sudden jumps are not.
Cooling system may overshoot by 0.5-1°C on the first cycle — observe for two readings before treating as an anomaly.
key_findings: Slow cooling at 0.5°C/hour produced crystal clarity of 94% — establishes baseline for KDP crystallization
Temperature held stable at 35.0°C ± 0.3°C throughout 8-hour run with zero critical excursions
Final impurity 18.2 ppm, well within 30 ppm target
No interventions required — all parameters remained within defined thresholds
